content.title: Response to Reviewer 9ecU
content.comment:
We would like to show our sincere gratefulness to review our paper and provide us good suggestion to polish our paper.

Question 1:

1.The technique novelty is limited. Converting timestamps as temporal convolutional filters to fully interact with entities and relations is a simple way.

Answer:

We feel sorry to bring the review an impression of lacking of novelty about our paper. Here we would like to re-state our modelling novelty and wish the reviewer would agree with us to some extent: 

(1) Generally speaking, there are mainly two ways to integrate the temporal information into the TKGC modellings: a) to integrate time information into entity embeddings: time only influences the characteristics or features of entities in facts, but has no impact on features relations; b) to integrate time information into relation embeddings: time only influences the characteristics of relations in facts, but does not change the features of entities. The design of TaCE firstly introduce the timestamps as the convolution filters to effectively interact with the entity and relation embeddings. Compared with those complex models composed of sequence model (such as LSTM or RNN) and GCNs, our convolution-based model behaves much efficient and light in computation. 

(2) Besides, a two-channel design, making the temporal convolution module co-work with the static module, allows our model to consider the cases with or without timestamps, considering that not all the facts does have to be changed with the time. In order to comprehensively integrate both static and temporal features, the deep learning module is further developed. Such designs are also ingenious. 

(3) Moreover, TaCE can easily incorporate additional properties such as spatial information or the entity descriptions to enhance the reasoning accuracy based on knowledge graph.

Question 2:

Experimental results are not enough. Wiki and Yago are two popular datasets for TKGE. The authors do not provide the results on these two datasets.

Answer:

Follow the reviewer’s advice, we have added new datasets including YAGO11k, WIKIDATA12k and YAGO15k into our experiment. Additional results are shown in Appendix A.1 which can prove the superiority of our TaCE.

content.title: Follow up
content.comment: Thank you again for your feedback on our paper. We would like to kindly ask if you have any additional comments on the updated manuscript, in particular regarding the additional datasets, yago and wiki, that we added based on your recommendation.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper998 by Reviewer yWGz

content.title: Response to Reviewer yWGz
content.comment:
We would like to show our sincere gratefulness to the reviewer for helping us polish our paper.

Question 1:

The model only works for discreet times due to the convolution and the proposed model structure, which limits the ability of real-world applications where a lot of temporal knowledge graphs have temporal intervals. A lot of recent papers also address temporal intervals in temporal knowledge graphs.

Answer:

Actually, TaCE has the ability to deal with the temporal knowledge graphs with temporal intervals. We conduct the experiments on YAGO11k and WIKIDATA12k, both of which are two popular public benchmarks with temporal intervals, the experimental results are shown in Appendix. The experiments shows that TaCE consistently achieves the best performance in terms of MRR, Hits@1 and Hits@3, which convincingly proves that TaCE can be applied on temporal knowledge graphs with temporal interval.

Here, we explain how to address the temporal intervals in a case of {Gavriel_Salvendy, works At, Tsinghua_University, 2001, 2011} based on YAGO11k by following steps:

(1) a temporal interval of (2001, 2011) is treated as two time stamps, namely, the start point 2001 and the end stamp 2011; 

(2) we obtain the start and end timestamp embeddings upon the timestamp, respectively;

(3) we compute a mean vector of the above two embeddings as the input timestamp embedding for the model. 

Question 2:

What about knowledge graphs with incomplete temporal information, e.g, some triples have temporal information while other triples are missing temporal information. Can the model handle these knowledge graphs? How is the performance?

Answer:

As TaCE owns a static convolution module, it has the capability to handle those knowledge graphs with incomplete temporal information. We just need to add a special and invalid timestamp ‘0000-00-00’ for the facts without time information; such an operation, following exactly the same way advised by TNTComplEx (2020), is to make the input quadruples satisfy the requirements for TaCE. Our further experiment can explain this point by involving YAGO15k dataset which is dominated 73.4% of the total triples without timestamps. Results show that, except for H@10, TaCE performs very closely to the best model (ChronoR) on MRR, Hits@1 and Hits@3. This convinces the capability of TaCE in handling the incomplete time information.

Question 3:

The paper seems to be missing the time prediction task that a lot of existing temporal knowledge graph embedding models evaluate on, for example, as reported in this paper (Temporal Knowledge Base Completion: New Algorithms and Evaluation Protocols).

Answer:

TaCE has a reasonably good temporal awareness (see Fig.6), but it cannot be easily adjusted to predict the time for a given event. We admit that it could be one shortage associated with our model. In TaCE, time information plays as the core input information to assist the model inferring the missing relation/entity. If we remove the temporal information out of our model, the temporal convolution module will be nonexistent, and thus our model is merely a convolution-based static knowledge reasoning model. In that case, our novelty in TaCE will be dismounted. Time predictability might be viewed as an important aspect to evaluate the KG reasoning task. However, whether we want make good use of the temporal information to serve a better prediction on entity/relation or reversely to predict time, it should meet what exactly the task needs for. Definitely, here the reviewer advises us another good point to work on in the future.

Question 4:

The experiment could be more convincing if it could include other knowledge graph datasets, such as wikidata12k and yago11k/yago15k.

Answer:

Follow the reviewer’s advice, we have added new datasets including YAGO11k, WIKIDATA12k and YAGO15k into our experiment. Results shown in in Appendix A.1 further prove the superiority of our TaCE.

content.title: Response to Reviewer yWGz
content.comment:
Question 1:

The way the time interval is handled is a bit naive. What about statements with multiple time intervals or discontinuous time intervals?

Answer:

By reviewing the previous researches to deal with the same situation, there are mainly two ways: 

1)	to discretize it into time particles along the time by TNTComplEx method [1]. For example, (A person, works At, Paris, [2001, 2015]) will be converted to (A person, works At, Paris, 2001), (A person, works At, Paris, 2002), …, (A person, works At, Paris, 2015), given that the temporal granule is set as a year.

2)	to separate it into two parts, namely, the start timestamp and the end timestamp, by TeRo method [2]. (A person, works At, Paris, [2001, 2015]) will be turned into (A person, works At, Paris, 2001) and (A person, works At, Paris, 2015);

The first operation will largely increase the size of the training set particularly when the fact has a long time span. Say (A person, Live, Paris, [1925, 2015]), there will be 90 extra instances added into the training dataset. We concern that will change the distribution of the training sets, and will further affect the sample distribution mapped into the high dimensional spaces. In that case, the inferencing results will be artificially changed.

Due to the input of the model requiring a fact with only one timestamp, we employ a strategy of computing the mean vector of the start and end time embeddings instead. This method will keep the training size the same as usual. 

As for the facts with multiple time intervals or discontinuous time intervals, they can be separated into numerous: for instance, (A person, works At, London, [2001, 2003], [2007, 2013], [2016, 2020]) will be converted to (A person, works At, London, [2001, 2003]), (A person, works At, London, [2007, 2013]) and (A person, works At, London, [2016, 2020]). After that, each separated fact will be processed as the aforementioned ways.

[1] Tensor decompositions for temporal knowledge base completion. International Conference on Learning Representations, 2020.

[2] Tero: A time-aware knowledge graph embedding via temporal rotation. Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computational Linguistics, 2020.

Question 2:

The results for YAGO and WIKIDATA are not as impressive.

Answer:

We have conducted the most extensive comparison involving six benchmarks and 14 baseline models. Such an extensive comparison allows us to draw the robustness and reliability of our model. Although the results of our model on YAGO and WIKIDATA are not as superior on ICEWS and GDELT, we still can bit SOTA on YAGO11k and WIKIDATA12k on the metrics of MRR, H@1 and H@3.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a novel temporal knowledge graph embedding approach that is based on convolutional neural networks. To create a feature on which the link prediction is performed, the presented approach first creates both a static and a temporal feature (both in their own respective convolution modules) and fuses them together in a third deep learning module. The so generated general feature is then used to calculate scores for the missing element in a tuple (s,r,o,t). The experimental section provides a performance overview of the proposed TaCE approach on standard benchmark datasets for TKGC tasks (ICEWS{14|05-15} and GDELD). As seen in the evaluation, the proposed approach performs better or on-par with most recent SOTA approaches in the field. The result presentation is followed by a more detailed analysis of the learned temporal embeddings that appear to contain a good semantic representation of temporal order. An ablation study further shows the huge impact that the temporal embedding module has on the overall results.
content.main_review:
+ the overall quality of presentation is very good. The paper and line of arguments are easy to follow

+ the presented approach is the first to apply convolutional neural networks in the context of a temporal knowledge graph completion task

+ the proposed approach generates better results on the benchmarks than most recent TKGE approaches

+ the qualitative analysis of the temporal embeddings indicate that meaningful semantics are learnt

- it is a bit unclear how the timestamps are represented initially; is the timestamp embedding a vector representation of a timestamp that is processed in the same way as the other entities (i.e. in a symbolic representation) or is there an additional step involved?

- can you explain in more detail how section 5.4. shows the ability of TaCE to provide order? Surely the example shows that quadruples belonging to ground truth, i.e. that are facts in the respective KG are assigned a high score by TaCE, but I do not see how in this case this necessarily is an indicator that the model has learnt the sequential relation between the quadruples. I agree that section 5.3. provides strong indicators that the semantics of the timestamps are well represented by your approach, but to me it remained unclear how section 5.4. further supports that claim. A more detailed explanation could – in my opinion – help clarifying this question
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors present TaCE, an approach for TKGC tasks that is based on the usage of convolutional neural networks. The novelity and the shown effectiveness of their approach plus the qualitative analysis of the temporal embeddings make this paper a clear accept. Not only do the authors provide a performant approach, but they also aim to explain the effectiveness of their proposed approach.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper998 by Reviewer AUM2

content.title: Response to Reviewer AUM2 - Part 1 (1/2)
content.comment:
We would like to show our sincere gratefulness to the reviewer for providing us so many good points to help polish our paper. Some of them really enlighten us to formulate some new ideas about TKGC modelling.

Question 1:

[Title of the paper]: Claims TaCE does Temporal Knowledge "Reasoning" but the text don't justify the claim.

Answer: 

We really appreciate your careful reading and good suggestion. In essence, “knowledge graph completion” is actually doing the same job as “knowledge graph completion”, to “infer the missing component for facts given a knowledge graph” [1]. However, it is true that we only mentioned the “reasoning” in our title but went with the “completion” throughout the text. To make the title consistent with the whole text, we would make it clear that in our text that the “reasoning” and “completion” can be replaceable. The adding information has been highlighted by yellow in Section 1 & 3.

reference:

 [1] A review: Knowledge reasoning over knowledge graph[J]. Expert Systems with Application, 2020, 141(Mar.):112948.1-112948.21.

Question 2:

Qualitative study on what type of cases TaCE performs better than the competing model will strengthen the claim of the need for a more expressive model.

Answer:

We are not very sure that if the reviewer wants to see a comparison between our model and the compellers in Sec.5. 4. We actually have thought about this point when we design the test. However, due to the different score functions used by different modelers, it makes the final probability incomparable among the TKGC models. For example, TNTComplEx (2020) plots the probability for {President of the French republic, office holder, ?} in the scale of [7.5,16.0]; TIMEPLEX (2020) projects a similar case study about the probability projection over a range of [-0.01, 0.02]. It would definitely affect the conclusion. That is why we did not make a parallel comparison in our case study. Suggested by other reviewers, we further add another three datasets for quantitative comparison. Please go Appendix A.1 for a review.

Question 3:

Table 3: TaCE w/o temporal component performs better than ConvE, while the underlying principle of both the models is similar. Why is TaCE better? Comments?

Answer:

This an interesting question. By removing the temporal component from TaCE, the model only has the static convolution module to work with the deep learning component to draw the final prediction. We would draw that TaCE has such small advantages over ConvE on is mainly due to the existence of the deep learning module, which can learn a better representation through the hidden layers. Another possible reason could be the different ways to layout the relation and entity embeddings. TaCE vertically stacks the two vectors while ConvE concatenates the relation embedding vector with the entity’s in a plane. This may contribute to slightly different filters during the training process and thus the compound representations for entities and relations. As there is no comparison study by far on how to effectively layout the entity and relation embeddings, it may introduce another deliberate experiment to make a proof.

Question 4:

Any specific reason for not sharing entity and relation embeddings used in temporal and static modules? Comment on the performance, space, and speed requirements of the new model – TaCE. Along with Table 2 and Table 4, also consider reporting the size of the corresponding models.

Answer:

We concerns two reasons for not sharing entity and relation embeddings used in temporal and static modules. First, by doing that it may undermine their own capability in distinguishing corresponding features to some extent. The temporal embeddings are supposed to solely capture the dynamic features drawn from the time-evolving entities and relations, so do the static embeddings. The performance of TaCE would drop by around 2% by sharing the same entity and relation embeddings in two different modules. Second, using shared embeddings would slow down the whole training process. This has been ascertained by a test on ICEWS14: to achieve exactly the same high performance, the model with shared embedding consumes at least twice time to finish the task compared with the opposite operation. 

The reviewer may concern that the strategy for not sharing entity and relation embeddings would increase the model size. We attach a table, Appendix A.5, comparing the model size (reflected by the total number of parameters) associated with the typical TKGC models. The size of TaCE is smaller than ChronoR (2021) and TNTComplEx (2020). TIMEPLEX (2020) has the largest size.

content.title: Response to Reviewer AUM2 - Part 2 (2/2)
content.comment:
Question 3:

Some real examples from datasets highlighting the cases where TaCE performs better than the competing model will strengthen the claim of the need for a more expressive model.

Answer:

Thanks for your suggestion. We have explained the hardships of doing such a case comparison in our qualitative study. Hope the review can understand. 

Question 4:

There is no comment on code release from the authors (even after a fellow reviewer raised the issue). Without code, it is hard to reproduce the results reported.

Answer:

We understand the reviewer’s concerns. For the sake of protecting our method, we are more comfortable to release our codes once our paper gets accepted. Hope reviewers could understand us at this point. 

Question 5:

Regarding response on technical novelty question: (a) Previous models like -- TNTComplEx(2020) and TIMEPLEX (2020) incorporate time information in entity and relation embeddings. (b) Previous temporal KBC models also worked with missing time information by learning an OOV vector.

Answer:

Here, we may have different views about time incorporation with the reviewer. The time incorporation we mean here should base on the definition or an assumption that whether the relations or entities (or both) are affected by time. In our case, we regard the relations and entities are co-changed with time; so we design the timestamps as the convolution filter to interact with relation and entity embeddings. In TNTComplEx (2020), the authors define the relation to be time-aware; so the time information is first assigned to the relation embeddings for integration; then the time-aware relation embeddings will be interacted with the entity embeddings. In that case, we regard TNTComplEx into the group——“to integrate time information into relation embeddings”. For TIMEPLEX, the authors did not define in the text that whether the relations or the entities are regarded as temporally varied; the multiplication of the time vector with the vectors of <s,r>, <o,r>, <s,o> does not require the authors to consider the order for relation or entity. We regards TIMEPLEX being out of the two typical cases presented in our answer.

In terms of using OOV vector for missing information, this is mentioned nowhere in our answering. This is definitely not equivalent to our idea of modelling static knowledge graph. We are not sure why the reviewer raise this point. We assume there must be another misunderstanding.

content.title: Response to Reviewer AUM2 - Part 1 (1/2)
content.comment:
Question 1:

Experiments on Yago11k, Yago15k, and Wikidata12k: TaCE scores aren't impressively superior to the score of competing models. Moreover, it lags behind TIMEPLEX and ChronoR on some parameters.

Answer:

We have conducted the most extensive comparison involving six benchmarks and 14 baseline models. Such an extensive comparison allows people to catch a full glimpse at the robustness and reliability of our model. Although our model lags behind TIMEPLEX and ChronoR on some metrics, we still can bit them on YAGO11k and WIKIDATA12k on metrics of MRR, H@1 and H@3. That may not prove our model superiority, but at least to be competitive. Due the TIMEPLEX did not test on GDELT and YAGO15k, and ChronoR missed the datasets of GDELT, YAGO11k and WIKIDATA12k, we cannot make a full observation about them. However, large enhancement on ICEWS14, ICEWS05-15 and GDELT would make us be confident about the advantage of our model on reasoning on event datasets.

Question 2:

It is unclear why a mean vector of the start and end time embeddings is the best way to represent the time interval. 

Answer:

We would not say “the mean vector of the start and end time embeddings” is the best way to represent the time interval, but it is a practical way. Reviewing the previous researches to deal with the time interval, there are mainly two ways:

1)	to discretize it into time particles along the time by TNTComplEx method [1]. For example, (A person, works At, Paris, [2001, 2015]) will be converted to (A person, works At, Paris, 2001), (A person, works At, Paris, 2002), …, (A person, works At, Paris, 2015), given that the temporal granule is set as a year.

2)	to separate it into two parts, namely, the start timestamp and the end timestamp, by TeRo method [2]. (A person, works At, Paris, [2001, 2015]) will be turned into (A person, works At, Paris, 2001) and (A person, works At, Paris, 2015). TeRo scores the fact with time interval at start and end timestamp respectively, and get the mean value of the two scores to represent the probability of the fact;

The first operation will largely increase the size of the training set particularly when the fact has a long time span. Say (A person, Live, Paris, [1925, 2015]), that will be 90 extra instances to be added into the training dataset. We concern that will change the instance distribution of the training fact, and will further affect the distribution mapped into the high dimensional spaces. In that case, the inferencing results will be artificially changed.

Due to the input of the model requiring a fact with only one timestamp, we employ a strategy of computing the mean vector of the start and end time embeddings instead. This method will keep the training size the same as usual. 

[1] Tensor decompositions for temporal knowledge base completion. International Conference on Learning Representations, 2020.

[2] Tero: A time-aware knowledge graph embedding via temporal rotation. Proceedings of the 28th International Conference on Computational Linguistics, 2020.

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer AUM2 - Part 1 (1/2)

content.title: Response to A2
content.comment: wrt A2: The authors may also want to look at TimePlex, which samples a time point uniformly at random from the query time interval [tb, te] associated with the fact. The method of sampling is efficient as the data size is unchanged. It also ensures each fact is sampled uniformly, not hurting link prediction performance by oversampling of long-duration facts.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper998 by Reviewer AUM2

content.title: Response to Reviewer AUM2 - Part 2 (2/2)
content.comment:
Question 5:

”Awareness of time ordering and consistency”: The heading of the qualitative study suggested that the authors are going to talk about how well does the model understands which relations come before another (a time-aware model should understand that a person has to be born before he becomes the president). The authors may consider re-evaluating their choice of heading.

Answer:

We feel sorry that the original version of Section 5.4 might be confusing in terms of its heading and text. In the current version, we have changed its heading with its text also revised. Hope this version would make this qualitative study clearly stated.

Question 6:

One disadvantage of such a convolution-based model is that they can’t naturally predict time while the discussed tensor-based models can. What are the author's thoughts? Is there an efficient way to do time prediction? And how well does the model do in this task?

Answer:

We agree with the reviewer at the point. Compared with the tensor-based models, the convolution-based models would face a shortage of unable to do time prediction. Being a convolution-based model, TaCE has to turn the timestamps into a convolution filter to interact with the relation and entity embeddings. Although it has reasonably good time awareness (shown in Fig.6), but it may not be easily adjusted its current structure to predict the timestamps for a given event. Here, the reviewer provide another angle for us to look at the temporal reasoning/completion task as well as to evaluate the models. Honestly, we have not got any good idea to efficiently dealing with time prediction in such a short time yet. But we may work on this direction in our future work.

Question 7:

Minor mistakes in paper writing and update bibliography.

Answer:

We appreciate the reviewer’s careful reading. We have gone through the entire article to correct the writing mistakes, and we also have updated the Arxiv articles replaced by their latest bibliographies.
